holidays.name: National Devil's Food Cake Day
holidays.description: A day to indulge in the rich, dark, chocolatey layer cake that is the sinful sibling of angel food cake. Frosting is practically mandatory.
holidays.origin: Devil's food cake first appeared in American cookbooks in the early 1900s, with the name likely coined to contrast it with the pale, airy angel food cake. The cake day is an unofficial food observance that popped up in the modern era of national food days.
holidays.funFact: Early devil's food cakes got their reddish tint from a chemical reaction between cocoa and baking soda, which is why some old recipes are famously red-brown.

holidays.name: National Pick Strawberries Day
holidays.description: A day for heading to the field, basket in hand, to harvest juicy red strawberries, then eating about half of them before you reach the car.
holidays.origin: This unofficial food and agriculture observance falls in late spring, when strawberries ripen in many parts of the United States and U-pick farms open for the season.
holidays.funFact: The strawberry is the only fruit with its seeds on the outside, averaging around 200 seeds per berry. Botanically, those seeds are the actual fruits.

holidays.name: International Museum Day (approx.)
holidays.description: Museums around the world open their doors with special events, late-night hours, and free admission, celebrating everything from priceless art to deeply odd collections of buttons and spoons.
holidays.origin: The International Council of Museums (ICOM) established the observance in 1977 to raise awareness of the role museums play in society. It is held annually on May 18, and in many places the festivities spill over into the following days, including May 19.
holidays.funFact: Some of the world's quirkiest museums include a museum of broken relationships in Zagreb, a museum of bad art in Massachusetts, and an instant ramen museum in Japan.

holidays.name: Malcolm X Day
holidays.description: A day honoring the birthday of civil rights leader Malcolm X, marked with educational events, discussions, and reflection on his legacy and influence on Black activism and identity.
holidays.origin: Malcolm X was born on May 19, 1925, in Omaha, Nebraska. Various communities and organizations commemorate his birthday every year, and some places have recognized it officially.
holidays.funFact: He was born Malcolm Little and later became El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz. His autobiography, written with Alex Haley, is one of the most widely read nonfiction books of the 20th century.

holidays.name: National Quiche Lorraine Day
holidays.description: A salute to the savory French custard tart, traditionally packed with bacon, eggs, and cream. Real men may or may not eat it, but everyone should.
holidays.origin: Quiche Lorraine hails from the Lorraine region of northeastern France, and its name comes from the German word 'Kuchen,' meaning cake. Its American popularity exploded in the 1950s, and a day was eventually set aside for it among unofficial food holidays.
holidays.funFact: The original Lorraine recipe had no cheese at all. Adding Gruyère or Swiss came later, and purists still argue about it.
